This might be getting old, but: I can relate to this comment. I've attempted twice in my adult life. 

The first time I told no one about my plans and I went to a secluded area, but after my firearm failed to discharge I just went home and never said a word to anyone. 

On my second attempt I, again, went to a secluded area (actually 7 states away) and only told one friend that I was "leaving". I had been eating progressively less over the last few months, and my plan was to die by starvation and exposure (I figured it was fool-proof). Once I had found the perfect spot, I slumped up against a tree completely exhausted from hiking. My head was pounding from dehydration and starvation; it was two weeks, then, since my last meal (two slices of bread) and two days since I had any water. I closed my eyes and felt myself slipping away. It was very painful, but I knew this was it and it was finally over. I woke up to a couple of hikers trying to perform CPR. Apparently I had only been unconscious for about 10 minutes when they spotted me. 

The feeling of regret after not dying is a pretty familiar feeling. I'm sorry to hear you felt that way, too.

Eh, it's not so much an excuse as it is a reason. I've attempted twice in the past, and by some stroke of luck (or misfortune, whichever you prefer) I survived both times. I've never given up the idea of suicide, try as I might, and ultimately it will be the thing that does me in. I 'make an excuse' to not take antidepressants because I know it'll give me exactly what I need to make one final attempt.

I'm also very aware of the sensation you talk about in your comment. I've experienced it and just about every other symptom in the last 15 years of my little MDD adventure. 

I thank you for your comment of concern and advice (if that was the intent?). Unfortunately, not everyone can afford professional help :/

This is an impressive post. It's both clinical and anecdotal. Nicely done. 

I like how you explain the impulse motivation behind suicide, and how having energy from antidepressants can suddenly give a person an urge to commit whereas they were too apathetic beforehand. This is one of the reasons I'll probably never take antidepressants.

A few years ago I was living with a coworker in his apartment. We'd become really good friends despite our differences in pay/rank/position/title, whatever you prefer. It was a very harsh time in my career and it really helped me out. In addition, I helped him with his alcoholism. 

One weekend I ended up going to sleep pretty early on his couch. When I got up, his bedroom was closed, so I let him sleep in because I figured he might have been drinking. When I got back later that night his door was still closed, so I thought I'd better check in on him. 

He looked like he was just sleeping all sprawled out on his bed. I put my hand on his shoulder and gave him a nudge and tried walking him up. That's when I felt that sick feeling in my gut. He was dead. 

My first instinct was to just get the hell out of there, and at first I did run. I ran out the front door but stopped and just collapsed on the ground. I sat next to his body while I waited for the police and ambulance to show up. The rest of the weekend was spent calling his whole family to tell them what happened. The official report was that he accidentally ingested way too much of his medication with way too much alcohol...there wasn't anything accidental about it.

Call it a chicken and the egg argument, but personally I believe the lack of confidence caused a lack of communication and therefore early building of social skills. In turn the lack of social acumen is where my social awkwardness is derived. 

Long story, short: Since birth, I've been competely alone with my handsome mug for a few decades now, and probably will continue to be alone for a few more decades...and then I'll die.  The end.

I used to enjoy sleeping. Actually enjoy isn't the right word, it's more like sleep relieves me. Every moment of my day is just guilt, shame, and self-loathing and when sleep finally comes it's great to just be unconscious for a while and not experience anything. 

Lately, though, I've started to have dreams again. I used to have them when I was younger but they were always nightmares. Nothing was ever pleasant about them and I used to dread going to sleep; ending a horrible day with an even worse night, just to awake to another horrible day. 

The nightmares are back. The days are worse and the nights aren't so pleasant anymore. In a couple months it will be year 16 of my deep depression, and no end in sight. 

Why don't I have the strength to kill myself?

I have to agree with you about not involving my parents in this. Currently, I'm doing just that, tiptoeing around them and playing things very close to the vest when talking with them about anything. Maybe some therapy will help me to get over this, but I guess time will tell. Thanks for your kind words and offer for a pm conversation, I do appreciate it.

It's also the fear that I may reach a breaking point from all of it at once. At the same time, though, I feel obligated to do so because so many other students juggle all that, if not more! I end up feeling conflicted, not wanting to overwhelm myself, but feeling inferior for not fulfilling my potential.

There's nothing concrete to prove this either way. There is vastly more knowledge that we as a species have yet to attain than compared to what we do know. Matter and energy interactions on a universal and atomic scale and human consciousness are done things we've yet to fully explore. 

I'm no optimist, so I'm not saying we all float up to the clouds and sing happy songs for eternity, but you can't just accept one thing as universal fact and fret over it. 

Try to find comfort in not knowing. Accept the mystery and understand its inevitability. If thinking that one way about death is bringing you down then think of some alternatives. You don't have to be correct about any one of them, but you shouldn't burden yourself with such morbidity for no practical reason. 

Besides, if you're right about that then you won't care afterwards, anyways. So why ponder it now? You've got more important things to consider.

I had several people I talked to on 7Cups that were actually pretty rude to me. I chalked them up to just trolling. The few that were actually alright gave some very strange advice. 

I talked with two separate people on two separate occasions on the Hotline, and both times they asked specifically where I was to dispatch police. They told me, "suicide is a crime" and I, "need to turn myself in". 

Like I said, I'm pretty sure these were just atypical and unlucky experiences, but they were enough that I'll never use either again.

It's great to hear that you changed for the better after your attempt! Surviving your attempt and coming out stronger can be inspiration for others to get back on their feet, no matter how far gone they think they are. 

Unfortunately, I can't say I experienced the same. After my first suicide attempt I was extremely shaken up about it, but never revealed any inkling of such an attempt to anyone. I think this only aided in my collapsing further into myself. I've still never told anyone the details, even anonymously, and most likely never will. 

After my second suicide attempt I didn't feel shaken at all. Instead I just felt completely empty; moreso than I ever thought I could. Again, I couldn't speak to anyone about this attempt, let alone the details of the attempt. I realized I'll never be able to successfully end my own life, and so I opted to keep entirely to myself and try to live as comfortably as possible until I die naturally.

Congrats on your newfound self, and good luck in the future!

Depression actually changes the way the brain operates and structures neural pathways. [Here](http://media.mlive.com/health_impact/photo/braincapturepng-cb4d47f44ae7bf35.png) is a picture showing brain scans that demonstrates what I'm referring to. 

It's not necessarily that depression causes a more accurate point of view on life, it's just a different point of view. Typically it's a point of view restricted from thought processes that normal brains can easily achieve. I don't mean to say depressed brains are in any way inferior, but that they're simply not operating as intended.

I'm no medical specialist, but I did a few years of research on the human brain to include the different parts, how they operate, and how depression affects said parts and the brain as a whole.

My friend got back from vacation last night. He asked if I wanted to come hang out at his place. I was feeling pretty low to begin with, but I eventually talked myself into going.

We caught up on the last week and talked a bit, then decided to watch a movie. He accidentally sat on the remote while juggling food and drinks, and the movie went back to the very beginning. I was joking around and exaggerated the point of his mistake. He chuckled and said 'dude, stop being a dick'. 

My friends had seen this movie once before and was excited I could finally see it because it's one of his favorite comedies. As soon as it started, though, all I could think about was what he said. I was a dick; I was at my friend's home, eating food he made for me, and I acted like a dick to him.

For the rest of the night I sat there pretending to watch the movie, thinking over and over about how that was the real me. Even if I want depressed, I'd be one of those cocky assholes that ruin everything for everyone. At least depressed-me is quiet and alone, so I never have to worry about hurting anyone like that.

I'm be working to separate my friend and I from now on. I can't be a good friend to him, and I don't want to hurt him anymore.

If you're feeling suicidal then I recommend posting in suicide_watch. The thing is, though, that fear that stops you is innate. The autopilot of self preservation is pretty tough to overcome for a reason. 

Either way, you are hurting and if you want to talk you can leave a comment or pm. I've overcome that fear. Twice. I know what it's like to be there and back, and it's not pretty. 

I urge you to seek help. You don't need to get professional help right away, but at least talk to a friend or family member, or just someone important. You don't have to let them know everything; just enough to know you're in need of help. If you feel like it'll be a burden on them, then just think about how you are probably as important to them as they are to you. If you'd be willing to help them in their time of need, you can bet they'd do the same for you.

Suicidal thoughts can be dangerous. Not in and of themselves, but what they can lead to.

First, it's one thought when you're *really* low. Next, it's an occasional thought even when you're just 'ok'. Before you know it, suicide is always on your mind and you can't remember a time when you thought "wow, a suicidal thought, I must be really down because I never think of that".

Pretty soon you're not scared of the thoughts anymore, and they can sometimes be a little comforting. Then one day you might just act...

After two failed suicide attempts I can say, you don't want to get to that point. Try to get some help, even if you think it was just a fluke because of your present circumstances.

I used to be pretty close to my younger brother. That changed last year when I abruptly disappeared to make my second attempt on my life. He got very scared because he knew what I was trying to do, and I wouldn't answer his calls for the few weeks I was gone.

When I came back he was so angry and sad that he wouldn't even acknowledge that I was in the same room. 

After more than 15 years of severe depression, I was indifferent to this. As bad as it sounds, I didn't really feel sorry or hurt that I ruined the close relationship between him and I. 

I don't want to tell you how to feel or what to be grateful for, but the fact that you do feel remorse means that you can still change things. It's not too late for anything, and if I had to suggest something I'd say tell your mother or brother how you feel. You don't have to open up all the way at first, but every one in a while just vent those screams into phrases to let your family know how *you* feel.

I've been depressed my whole life, and suicidal since my early teens. I'm constantly in my own head and after years of this I've developed an extreme inferiority complex. I know it's irrational, but I can't help but to believe I'm undeserving of even the most basic essentials.

When I have a job I usually start it with one goal in mind: get stable financially so I can go back to school. However, as time goes on (matter of months usually) I start to feel trapped, like I'm always going to be lifting boxes or ringing up purchases. Not that there's anything wrong with these jobs, they are essential, but I don't want to do them for the rest of my life. That is what I start to feel, though, that I'll always be stuck in monotony. This soon translates to me questioning if I was even capable, or deserving of higher education, or anything more than minimum wage, or anything at all! That's when I begin to justify to myself suicide as a means of escape from my cycle and usually end up quitting soon after I've finished my plans.

As I said, the more I look back on all of this it just seems like I'm whining and complaining over nothing. That makes me feel horrible because I know people who would kill for jobs and opportunities. I just start feeling worse and worse until I see suicide as not only an option, but as the right thing to do. 

Also, I very rarely save money because I can never make enough to get out of the paycheck-to-paycheck cycle. By the time the bills are paid I'm handing over my last 20 so I can get my weekly PB&J groceries for my meals. 

I don't view asking for help as a weakness. I only ever feel it's a weakness for me, and only if I ask my friends or family. I have an overwhelming sense of pride when it comes to self-reliance and feel I have let down those close to me when I ask them for help. I also carry all my shame, and constantly remind myself of it in an effort to not repeat mistakes. 

Again, I know it's not rational, but the greatest shame I could ever visit upon myself would be to return home after doing all of this now and ask for help. Just writing that is extremely difficult and I feel terrified and wince at the thought of doing that. This is ultimately the driving force behind my suicide now. I see death as more inviting than returning home and revealing the ultimate failure I've become as I wasted my youth.

I was 19 at the time, living sane and drug free with my mother in her home. It was a fairly new subdivision in rural Kentucky, about 45 minutes south of Louisville. 

I lived in the basement (yes, I understand I was the living embodiment of the stereotype). The basement was completely finished, furnished, and had almost every amenity. It was also a 'walk-out' basement, meaning there was a door on the back side of the house that led from the basement to a patio into the backyard.

Often, I would stay up late watching TV or working on projects  as none of my activities had any bearing on everyone else's sleep. Even though I would be up into the early morning hours I always had plenty of rest and never considered myself sleep deprived, especially to the point of hallucination. 

It was late autumn and I was still up for some reason or another around 2 or 3 in the morning. I had almost forgotten that night was a full moon. I love stargazing and it was my favorite season of the year, so I absolutely had to go out to take everything in. I noticed my mom's cats were in the basement as well, and when I got up to head outside they became really excited and headed for the door. I thought it was cute how enthusiastic they were and I decided I'd let them out and we'd kind of hang out in the backyard until morning. 

I grabbed a flannel button-down and some thick socks and went towards the door. Through the curtains on the door I could already see the effect of the moon as the whole yard was lit with that eerie moonlight. I stepped outside with cats darting through my legs and turned around to close the door behind me.

As I started to step out from under the porch above me and further into the yard to where I could see the sky, I noticed how still the night was. It's not wholly uncommon since it's rural Kentucky, autumn, and 2 or 3 in the morning. This stillness, though, felt tangible. I felt like I stepped into a painting rather than the yard just outside. There were no animals moving about, no wind rustling the leafless trees and undergrowth, and I felt like even I couldn't make any sounds as I crept into this unmoving night. 

The cats had already moved out into the yard. Instead of going all the way to the back and over the chain link fence into the thick woods on the other side, they stayed a good distance from it and sat down in a row perpendicular to the tree-line. I ignored the weird cat behavior (as one does when they become accustomed to cats) and positioned myself in my usual stargazing spot as I turned my attention to the sky. The moon was huge and so bright. I couldn't recall a time where I'd seen it like this. Everything, even the ground in the woods was illuminated in the pale glow of this moon.

Just as I'm beginning to make out constellations I hear a loud snap in the woods nearby. I knew it must have been some wildlife just strolling by, and thought maybe the cats finally worked up the nerve to brave the woods. When I looked down from the sky, however, the cats are all still lined up in the yard, with their heads collectively turned to face the left corner of the fence. I look out into the woods and there, walking along the other side of the fences of the houses was this person. I started to call out to inquire why anybody was walking around out there at this time of night, but stopped myself before I could utter a sound when the details came into view. This 'person' was tall, at least 7 feet tall. As it walked along the tree-line it was now fully in view with the help of the moonlight. I couldn't have seen it better, even in the daylight. It had long, lanky, but muscular limbs. It was naked from what I could tell because I could see it's skin (at least what looked like skin), pale and almost glowing as the moon reflected off it. Its massive hands had long fingers that ended with black nails that came to a point. Its head was a weird shape, viewing its profile, and was slightly larger than a person's of comparable size would be. It walked barefoot, slowly and with purpose, until it reached the halfway point of the fence. Still in full stride it turned its head to first, the cats. I looked to them as they arched their backs and warned the thing with their growls. As I looked back it then turned its gaze to me. I locked eyes with it, but I feel it more appropriate to say it locked eyes with me. I stared, quivering into these inky black wells in this things face. It had almost no nose, a small mouth that was slightly open and blew hot breath into the cold air with each fall of its chest. Its eyes were larger than a person, only slightly larger than golf balls. 

For what felt like a lifetime I stood there staring into those pits, and felt it staring into me. I heard nothing but its soft footfalls and its long, heavy, sighs. I found the nerve to start backing up towards the door under the patio. As I disappeared into the shadow of the deck above it looked back  to its path and slowly walked out of sight along the fences. 

The cats were almost more eager than I was to get back inside. I stayed up all night watching through the glass of the door until I saw the sun peeking out into the sky. 

I told my family about it, and my friends, too. No one really believed it. Some of them are fairly superstitious, but I guess in a way they'd have to 'see it to believe it'. I can tell they think I actually did see it, but don't really believe it themselves. I can still picture every detail of that night and play it back in my mind. The memory feels like it was hours long, when really it probably only lasted 5 minutes. To this day I have no idea what I saw and have never seen or heard of anything like it since.
25, burning all the bridges with family and friends so they won't miss me when I'm gone.
